source_text: ΛΟΓΟΣ Λ ʹ. Εἰς ἑαυτὸν, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς λέγοντας ἐπιθυμεῖν αὐτὸν τῆς καθέδρας Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, καὶ εἰς τὴν τοῦ λαοῦ προθυμίαν, ἣν ἐπεδείξαντο εἰς αὐτόν. Αʹ. Ἐγὼ θαυμάζω, τί ποτέ ἐστιν ὃ πρὸς τοὺς ἐμοὺς πεπόνθατε λόγους, καὶ πόθεν τοσοῦτον ἥττησθε τῆς ἡμετέρας φωνῆς, τῆς ὑπερορίου καὶ μι κρᾶς ἴσως, καὶ οὐδὲν ἐχούσης ἐράσμιον, ὥστε ταυτόν μοι δοκεῖτε πρὸς ἡμᾶς πεπονθέναι, ὃ πρὸς τὴν μαγνῆτιν λίθον τὰ σιδήρια. Ἐμοῦ τε γὰρ κρέμασθε, καὶ ἀλλήλων εἷς τοῦ ἑνὸς ἐχόμενοι, καὶ Θεοῦ πάντες, ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα, καὶ εἰς ὃν τὰ πάντα. Ὢ τῆς θαυμασίας ἁλύσεως, ἣν πλήκει τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον δεσμοῖς ἀλύτοις συνηρτισμένην! Τὸ δὲ αἴτιον, οὔτε τι οἶδα ἐγὼ τῶν ἄλλων σοφώτερον, ὅσα ἐμαυτῷ συνεπίσταμαι· εἰ μή τις τοῦτο αὐτὸ ἐμὴν σοφίαν ὑπολαμβάνει τὸ εἰδέναι, ὅτι μὴ σο φὸς εἴην, μηδὲ τῆς ἀληθινῆς καὶ πρώτης σοφίας ἐγγύς· ὃ πολλῷ δέουσι περὶ ἑαυτῶν ὑπολαμβάνειν οἱ νῦν σοφοί· ἐπειδὴ ῥᾷστον ἑαυτὸν ἀπατᾷν, καὶ οἴεσθαι εἶναί τι, οὐδὲν ὄντα, ὑπὸ τῆς κενῆς δόξης φυσώμενον. Οὔτε πρῶτος ὑμῖν τὸν τῆς ὀρθοδοξίας λόγον ἐκήρυξα, οὗ μάλιστα περιέχεσθε, ἴχνεσι δὲ ἀλλοτρίοις ἐπηκολούθησα, καὶ τούτοις ὑμετέ ροις· εἰρήσεται γὰρ τἀληθές· εἴπερ ὑμεῖς Ἀλεξάν δρου μαθηταὶ τοῦ πάνυ, τοῦ μεγάλου τῆς Τριάδος ἀγωνιστοῦ τε καὶ κήρυκος, καὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ τὴν ἀσέβειαν ἐξορίσαντος. Μέμνησθε γὰρ τῆς Ἀποστολικῆς ἐκείνης εὐχῆς, ἣ τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ἀσε βείας κατέλυσεν ἐν τόποις ἀξίοις τῶν τῆς γλώσσης ἀμαρευμάτων, ἵν' ὕβρις ὕβριν ἀμύνηται, καὶ στηλιτευθῇ θανάτῳ δικαίῳ θάνατος ψυχῶν ἄδικος. Βʹ. Οὐ ξένην οὖν πηγὴν ὑμῖν ἐῤῥήξαμεν, ὥσπερ ἣν Μωϋσῆς ἀνέδειξεν ἐν ἀνύδρῳ τοῖς ἀπ' Αἰγύπτου διωκομένοις, κεκρυμμένην δὲ καὶ συγκεχωσμένην ἀνεστομώσαμεν, κατὰ τοὺς παῖδας Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ μεγά λου, μὴ ὀρύσσοντας μόνον φρέατα ζῶντος ὕδα τος, ἀλλὰ καὶ φρασσόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν Φυλιστιαίων ἀνα καθαίροντας. Ἀλλ' οὐδὲ τῶν κομψῶν τις καὶ ἡδέων ἐγὼ, καὶ οἷος κολακείᾳ κλέπτειν τὴν εὔνοιαν· οἵους ὁρῶ πολλοὺς τῶν νῦν ἱερατεύειν ὑπισχνουμένων οἳ τὴν ἁπλῆν καὶ ἄτεχνον ἡμῶν εὐσέβειαν, ἔντεχνον πεποιήκασι, καὶ πολιτικῆς τι καινὸν εἶδος ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς εἰς τὰ ἅγια μετενηνεγμένης, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν θεάτρων ἐπὶ τὴν τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀθέατον μυσταγωγίαν· ὡς εἶναι δύο σκηνὰς, εἰ δεῖ τολμήσαντα τοῦτο εἰπεῖν, τοσοῦτον ἀλλήλων διαφερούσας, ὅσον τὴν μὲν πᾶσιν ἀνεῖσθαι, τὴν δὲ τισί· καὶ τὴν μὲν γελᾶσθαι, τὴν δὲ τιμᾶσθαι· καὶ τὴν μὲν θεατρικὴν, τὴν δὲ πνευματικὴν ὀνομάζεσθαι. Ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες, καὶ ὁ Θεὸς, φησὶν ὁ θεῖος Ἀπόστολος, ὡς οὐ ταύτης ἡμεῖς τῆς μερίδος, ἀλλ' οἷοι σκαιότητος ἂν θᾶττον καὶ ἀγροικίας, ἢ θωπείας καὶ ἀνελευθερίας ἔγκλημα δέξασθαι· οἵ γε καὶ πρὸς τοὺς λίαν ἀντεχομένους ἡμῶν ἔστιν ὅτε καὶ ὅπου φαινόμεθα τραχυνόμενοι, ἄν τι μὴ κατὰ λόγον ἡμῖν ποιεῖν νομίζωνται. Καὶ τοῦτο ἔδειξεν ἡ πρώην γενομένη περὶ ἡμᾶς καινοτομία, ἡνίκα ζήλῳ καὶ θυμῷ ζέσαντες ὑμεῖς ὁ λαὸς, βοῶντάς τε καὶ ὀδυρομένους ἐπὶ τὸν θρόνον τοῦτον ἐθήκατε, τὸν οὐκ οἶδ' εἴτε τυραννικὸν χρὴ λέγειν, εἴτε ἀρχιερατικόν· ἐθήκατε δ' οὖν, διὰ τὸν πό θον παρανομήσαντες.
thought_title: Why you hang on my plain words
orientation: Gregory, newly installed in Constantinople, opens by marveling at the people's love for his preaching and denying that it comes from his own wisdom.
pass_a_gloss: Speech 32. On himself, and to those saying he desires the see of Constantinople, and on the eagerness of the people, which they displayed toward him. 1. I marvel, what ever is it which you have experienced toward my words, and from where have you been so overcome by our voice, the foreign and small perhaps, and having nothing lovely, so that you seem to me to have experienced toward us the same thing as pieces of iron toward the magnet stone. For you hang from me, and each holding to one another, and all to God, from whom all things, and to whom all things. O the marvelous chain, which the Holy Spirit weaves, fitted together with unbreakable bonds. But the cause, I know nothing wiser than the rest, as far as I know myself. Unless someone supposes this itself to be my wisdom, to know that I am not wise, nor near the true and first wisdom. Which the present wise men are far from supposing about themselves. Since it is easiest to deceive oneself, and to think one is something, being nothing, puffed up by empty glory. Nor did I first preach to you the word of the orthodox faith, which you especially hold fast, but I followed foreign tracks, and these your own. For the truth shall be spoken. If indeed you are disciples of Alexander the excellent, the great champion and herald of the Trinity, who banished impiety by word and by deed. For you remember that apostolic prayer, which destroyed the originator of impiety in places worthy of the babblings of his tongue, in order that outrage may repel outrage, and the unjust death of souls may be exposed to public shame by a just death. 2. Therefore we did not burst open for you a strange spring, such as Moses displayed in a waterless place for those pursued from Egypt, but we opened again one that was hidden and stopped up, after the manner of the children of Isaac the great, who not only dug wells of living water, but also cleaned out again those being stopped up by the Philistines. But I am not one of the elegant and pleasant men, and such as to steal goodwill by flattery. Such as I see many of those now promising to perform priestly office, who have made our simple and artless piety artful, and a new kind of political thing transferred from the marketplace into the holy things, and from the theaters onto the worship unseen by the many. So that there are two stages, if one must dare to say this, differing from each other as much as that the one is open to all, but the other to some. And the one is laughed at, but the other is honored. And the one is called theatrical, but the other spiritual. You are witnesses, and God, says the divine Apostle, that we are not of this portion, but such as would sooner accept a charge of awkwardness and rusticity, than of fawning and illiberality. We who also at times and in places appear harsh even toward those most attached to us, whenever they are judged to do anything not according to reason toward us. And this showed the recent innovation concerning us, when you the people, boiling with zeal and anger, set on this throne, while shouting and mourning, one who I do not know whether one must call tyrannical, or high priestly. You set him however, having broken the law on account of longing.

pass_b_english: I marvel at what has come over you when you hear my words, and how my voice has so overcome you. It comes from abroad and it is small, I suppose, with nothing to attract love, yet you seem to act toward me as iron acts toward a magnet. You hang from me, and each of you holds to one another, and all of you hold to God, from whom are all things and to whom are all things (Romans 11:36). What a wonderful chain, fitted together with unbreakable bonds, which the Holy Spirit weaves!

But the cause is not wisdom: as far as I know myself, I know nothing wiser than anyone else, unless someone counts this itself as my wisdom: to know that I am not wise, and not even near the true and first wisdom. The wise men of today fall far short of such judgment about themselves, since nothing is easier than to deceive oneself and, puffed up by empty pride, to think he is something when he is nothing (Galatians 6:3). Nor was I the first to preach to you the word of the orthodox faith, which you hold so firmly. I followed in the footsteps of others, and those footsteps are your own. The truth shall be told: you are disciples of Alexander, that excellent man, that great champion and herald of the Trinity, who drove out impiety by word and deed. For you remember that apostolic prayer which destroyed the author of impiety in a place that matched the filth of his tongue, so that insult might answer insult, and the unjust death of souls might be exposed to public shame by a just death.

So we broke open for you no strange spring, like the one Moses revealed in the dry land for those driven out of Egypt. We opened again a spring that lay hidden and choked up, like the servants of the great Isaac, who not only dug wells of living water but also cleared out those the Philistines had stopped up (Genesis 26:18-19). Nor am I one of the clever and charming speakers who steal goodwill by flattery. I see many among those who now promise to serve as priests who have turned our simple and artless devotion into something artful. They have carried a new kind of public maneuvering from the marketplace into holy things, and from the theaters into the worship hidden from the many. The result is two stages, if I dare say so. They differ as much as this: the one is open to all and the other to a few, the one is laughed at and the other is honored, the one is called theatrical and the other is called spiritual.

As Paul the Apostle says, “You are witnesses, and God,” that we do not belong to that party. We would sooner be accused of clumsiness and roughness than of fawning and servility. Even toward those most devoted to us we sometimes appear harsh in some place and at some moment, when they seem to act unreasonably toward us. This was shown by the recent innovation carried out upon me, when you the people, burning with zeal and anger, set me shouting and wailing upon this throne, which I do not know whether to call tyrannical or priestly. Set me you did, breaking the law through longing.

problems.quote: As far as I know myself, I know nothing wiser than anyone else
problems.source_quote: Τὸ δὲ αἴτιον, οὔτε τι οἶδα ἐγὼ τῶν ἄλλων σοφώτερον
problems.why: The source names the cause of the people's attraction, and says it is not Gregory's wisdom. The English drops 'the cause', so the explanatory link to the preceding marvel is lost.
problems.fix: The cause is not wisdom: as far as I know myself, I know nothing wiser than anyone else, unless someone counts this itself as my wisdom: to know that I am not wise.
problems.ruling: Τὸ δὲ αἴτιον names the cause of their attraction; English omits it, so that explanatory link is lost.
